lesson.title: How a Bundle of Light Becomes a Picture of the World
lesson.summary: Vision begins with the eye converting light energy into neural signals through a chain of specialized structures whose differing sensitivities help explain classic findings about absolute threshold and low light detection.
lesson.body:
Light enters the eye through the cornea, a clear curved structure that begins bending, or refracting, light toward a focal point, then passes through the pupil, an adjustable opening whose size is controlled by the surrounding iris. Behind the pupil, the lens fine tunes that focus, changing shape to sharpen images of objects at different distances, a process called accommodation. All of this focusing exists to serve one destination: the retina, the light sensitive tissue lining the back of the eye, where light energy is finally converted into neural signals the brain can use, a process called transduction.

The retina contains two main types of photoreceptor cells, rods and cones, and their differing properties explain a great deal about how vision actually behaves. Cones are concentrated most densely in the fovea, a small central region of the retina, and they are responsible for color vision and fine detail, but they require relatively bright light to function well. Rods, far more numerous and spread across the peripheral retina, are exquisitely sensitive to dim light but cannot distinguish color and provide only coarse detail. This division of labor explains a common experience: in very dim light, colors seem to disappear and faint objects are easier to see out of the corner of the eye than by looking straight at them, because peripheral vision relies more heavily on the more light sensitive rods.

This rod and cone sensitivity difference is directly tied to Absolute Threshold. The classic illustration of a faint candle flame detected at a great distance on a clear dark night works precisely because rods can respond to remarkably small amounts of light, pushing the absolute threshold for vision under ideal, fully dark adapted conditions to an extraordinarily low level. Dark adaptation itself, the gradual increase in visual sensitivity that occurs over several minutes in a darkened environment, reflects rods slowly regenerating the light sensitive pigment that was bleached out by previous exposure to brighter light, a process that lowers the absolute threshold over time as adaptation proceeds.

Color vision depends on the three types of cones, each most sensitive to a different range of wavelengths corresponding roughly to red, green, and blue light, a foundation known as trichromatic theory. Signals from these cones are then further processed by opponent process mechanisms further along the visual pathway, which compare signals in paired channels such as red versus green and blue versus yellow, helping explain phenomena like afterimages, where staring at a saturated color and then looking at a blank white surface produces a fleeting image in the opposing color.

Finally, all of this neural information converges on the optic nerve, a bundle of axons that carries visual signals from the retina to the brain. The point where the optic nerve exits the eye contains no photoreceptors at all, creating a blind spot in each eye's field of view that goes unnoticed in ordinary vision because the brain fills in the missing information using surrounding visual context.
